extracted.intended_audience: instructional designers, online course developers, and distance-education practitioners (higher education)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, developing, and deploying high-quality online courses and Educational Social Software (ESS) in distance education contexts. Covers technical, pedagogical, institutional, privacy, and evaluation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional designs grounded in sound learning theories
rubrics_metrics.description: the instructional designs of the learning materials are stable because they have been based firmly on sound, proven learning theories
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should ensure course designs are theoretically informed and stable prior to developer work; designs should not be ad-hoc but aligned with accepted learning theory to support pedagogical decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet institutional internal and external quality, usability, interoperability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: these instructional designs will meet the institution’s identified and articulated internal and external standards for quality, usability, and interoperability
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course materials must conform to institutional/regulatory requirements (quality assurance, accessibility/usability, interoperability with other systems and standards). Consider organizational policies and external standards bodies when designing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate media to meet standards
rubrics_metrics.description: appropriate media have been selected to meet these standards
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose media types (text, audio, video, interactive simulations) deliberately to satisfy pedagogical goals and institutional standards rather than by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technologies should exploit media characteristics and not be superfluous
rubrics_metrics.description: the technologies selected for course delivery are not superfluous – rather, the course design will exploit the unique characteristics of the selected media to engage and support both learners and teachers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting technologies, ensure they add pedagogical value (accessibility, multimedia, hyperlinking, multiple/global perspectives, ease of revision, accommodation of interaction forms). Avoid adding tools that do not support learning goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs must be practical, cost-effective, and timely to develop
rubrics_metrics.description: the designs are practical and can be developed in a cost-effective and timely way
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance pedagogical ambition with realistic production schedules and budgets; prefer designs that can be implemented and maintained within institutional resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner profiles capture rich learner data
rubrics_metrics.description: systems might capture interests, learning styles, goals and aspirations, accomplishments, and progress through a course of studies; personal characteristics such as professional interest and experience; family status; and other individual and group information
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ESS/learner-modeling components to gather relevant profile data to enable personalization (e.g., interests, goals, progress). Use standards (XML-based profiles) to allow machine- and human-readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner control of profiles for trust and privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: learner profiles must be under the ultimate control of the learner if critical issues of trust and privacy are to be maintained in ESS systems
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give learners control over what profile information is shared and with whom; this is essential for trust and privacy and should be enforced by system design and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track activities and use referrals to guide learners
rubrics_metrics.description: ESS tools track activities which students engage in, noting indicators of success (time spent, assessments attempted and passed, formal evaluations, and so on). These referrals can be used by students to select learning activities and courses, and by teachers and administrators to evaluate, refine, and continuously improve the learning activities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement activity-tracking and use those signals to recommend resources/activities and to inform continuous improvement. Include indicators like time on task, assessment attempts, and formal evaluation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support implicit/stigmergic referral systems (activity trails)
rubrics_metrics.description: implicit referral systems in which students’ activities leave trails, much like the pheromone trails left by ants to guide other members ... simulations show how individual student experiences can be used to improve learning networks and provide useful referral services to new students
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems that expose activity trails (e.g., frequently used resources, successful pathways) to help newcomers discover effective resources and activities; consider models from stigmergy for social navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link resources with people who built/used/commented on them
rubrics_metrics.description: link resources with the humans who have built, used, recommended, or otherwise commented upon them. This explicit conjunction will facilitate much more fine-grained searches and allow systems where learners can meet with and engage with others based on their individual experience of learning activities and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metadata and user-contributed annotations should connect artifacts to authors, reviewers, and users to support discovery and social matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate introductions and community building via weak/strong ties
rubrics_metrics.description: mining both weak and strong connections allows us to become acquainted with, and possibly work or learn together with others, with a greater probability of developing profitable exchanges
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide social networking/referral features that exploit friends-of-friends and weak links to introduce learners to potential collaborators and communities of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support reputation-building and documented contribution trails
rubrics_metrics.description: ESS tools facilitate the development and sharing of reputation, since documented postings and interactions can be used as referencing trails to determine the past contribution of learners
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep persistent records of contributions and interactions so learners can build reputational capital; expose these trails to support selection of collaborators and recognition of contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support peer help mechanisms (e.g., agent-mediated I-Help)
rubrics_metrics.description: I-Help system configures an autonomous agent that knows its owner’s skills, preferences, and fiscal capacity to provide and request help from other students; negotiations may lead to requests for help and evaluation by both helper and helped
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include peer-help workflows and (optionally) agent mediation to match seekers and helpers, include means for exchange and mutual evaluation. Design for authenticity while guarding against misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and mitigate misuse (cheating/plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: help can also be used for activities that violate academic standards and morals, such as cheating and plagiarism ... technical and social fixes have been developed to at least partially constrain these opportunities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement technical controls, policy, assessment design (e.g., competency-type examinations), and social norms to reduce opportunities for cheating while leveraging social learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support documenting, sharing, and continuous updating of learner-created content
rubrics_metrics.description: ESS tools will need to support students working continuously to update content that was initiated months or even years before by other students. Wikis and collaborative blogs are first-generation tools ... more sophisticated tools are needed, capable of including multimedia, tracking both contributor and learner use, controlling access to creation tools, and assessing learning outcomes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide collaborative authoring environments that allow versioning, multimedia, contributor tracking, usage analytics, access control, and assessment of resulting learning objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design learning objects to be shareable, reusable, and repurposable
rubrics_metrics.description: learning objects are designed to be shareable, reusable, and repurposed so that they can work in multiple contexts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt standards and modular design for learning objects to maximize reuse across courses and contexts (metadata, packaging, granularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: ESS feature set (blogging, portfolios, discussion, file sharing, search/linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: ESS tools ... offer combinations of blogging, portfolio management, discussion and file sharing, group file management, and search and linking capacity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize inclusion of these core social features where pedagogically justified and ensure they interoperate smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer open-source platforms for customization, security, and control
rubrics_metrics.description: proprietary offerings provide a service, but not distributing the software itself ... they do not allow the freedom to design and create value-added instances ... nor do they provide the type of security and control demanded by many formal education institutions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When institutional customization, security, and control are priorities, consider open-source ESS platforms to allow adaptation and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide fine-grained privacy/access controls
rubrics_metrics.description: ELGG has what we believe to be the most versatile privacy control system ... display of every field of information in a learner’s profile, plus all the items in their e-portfolio and their blog postings, can be restricted to only the author, their friends, particular communities, logged-on members, or the general public
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement configurable privacy settings per item/profile field to allow learners to manage visibility (author-only, friends, groups, members, public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate notification mechanisms (RSS, alerts) so learners need not wait
rubrics_metrics.description: these environments should support RSS and other notification tools such that learners are not expected to spend a great deal of time waiting for action on their institutional ESS installation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely notifications (RSS, email, push) to keep learners informed about activity and reduce latency in social interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow student customization and increasing control (PLE aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: this development will allow for very fine-tuned customization of learning contexts, not just by teachers and administrators, but by students, as they gain control over their own learning environments
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for learner personalization and empowerment, enabling students to tailor interfaces, resources, and social connections (subject to institutional constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select LMS/PLE tools appropriate to required document control and learner management
rubrics_metrics.description: personal learning systems do not offer the types of document control and learner management currently built into LMS systems
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When document control, secure assessments, or centralized learner management are priorities, prefer LMS capabilities; when learner-centered, networked learning is the priority, consider PLE/ESS approaches or hybrid models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mixed-methods pilot evaluation to develop grounded theory
rubrics_metrics.description: use a variety of data sources (interviews, observations, final exam scores, completion rate data, student perceptions of learning, cost accounting, machine-log analysis, and transcript analysis) to develop and test a grounded theory of educational social software use
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During pilot phases, collect qualitative and quantitative data (the list above) to iteratively refine design and to build explanatory theory about ESS efficacy and implementation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refine evaluation tools and validate theory across contexts in scale-up
rubrics_metrics.description: the evaluation tools that have proved most useful in pilot testing and development in Phase 3 will be refined and used to gather data across diverse sites. And the theory that has emerged in Phase 3 will be validated, tested, and refined in this phase
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In broader rollouts, standardize successful evaluation instruments and validate emergent theories with multiple partners and contexts; iterate based on cross-site findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose course type: text-based with enhancements vs. fully Internet-native distributed courses
rubrics_metrics.description: two basic categories: courses that are primarily text-based (with computer-mediated enhancements) and courses that are designed specifically for the distributed Internet setting, merging several smaller educational components into a single course of study
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to convert existing text materials with enhancements or to design a multi-modal Internet-native course; the choice affects pedagogy, production, and student expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chunk text and use multi-modal components in Internet-native courses
rubrics_metrics.description: in first-generation Internet-based courses text generally appears in short, concise 'chunks' and instruction is distributed among other multimedia components
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing Internet-native materials, break text into short segments and combine with multimedia learning objects, interactive activities, and other non-textual media to exploit web strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide essential administrative orientation documents to students
rubrics_metrics.description: your course should contain certain administrative documents to help instructors organize, prepare, and orient students ... these documents could include: personalized letter of welcome; general information about online learning, technology requirements, and available resources; information on how to access the course and navigate it; student log-in/password info; rules and procedures for interactive tools; course syllabus, overview, schedule, required texts, prerequisites, expectations, instructions on activities/assignments/deadlines; faculty contact information and office hours; student support information; administrative regulations including guidelines on plagiarism, privacy, appeals, library and counselling access
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make these materials easily accessible (preferably public pages for syllabus) so students can prepare before registration; be explicit about expectations, technical requirements, support, and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional model/infrastructure must support web-based instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: the fundamental requirement to gain support for web-based instruction from faculty, administrators, and students is an institutional model that is distinct from the traditional instructional-planning model and supports the design, development, and implementation of high-quality instruction on the Internet
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish institutional processes, staffing, support, policy, and governance tailored to online course development rather than relying solely on traditional models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty, administrators, and students must be assured of viability (faculty buy-in)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of these stakeholder groups – faculty, administrators, and students – must be assured that web-based instruction is a viable means of delivering courses and programs, and of accommodating student needs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence, pilot results, clear policies, and support resources to secure stakeholder buy-in; address concerns about workload, quality, and student outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage LMS features appropriate to the course
rubrics_metrics.description: most LMSs afford developers the use of text; email; asynchronous discussion boards; synchronous utilities such as VoIP; instant-messaging chat features; desktop and application sharing; on-demand video clips and demonstrative animations; interactive activities, simulations, and games; self-grading exercises, quizzes, and examinations; and secure assignment 'drop boxes'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select LMS features aligned with learning activities (synchronous vs asynchronous, assessment needs, collaboration); ensure they are configured and supported for intended pedagogical use.
